The estimation of interaction and quadratic effects in regression models with observed variables is a well-known procedure behavioral and social sciences [@aiken_west_1991; @rimpler_etall_2025; @olvera_astivia_etall_2025]. In that case, an interaction is commonly calculated by the product of certain predictors, whereas a quadratic term involves the product of a predictor with itself. This allows researchers to study, for example, the dependency that one variable may have on the level of another variable [@mize_2019], given the functional form. In a structural equation model (SEM) we usually have a regression function with latent variables (i.e., latent variable model or structural part) [@bollen_1989]. The "triviality" of estimating interaction and quadratic effects in this setting goes away because the scores (i.e., the subject-specific values) on the latent variables are, at least at the time of measurement, unobserved [@bollen_hoyle_2012]. Thus, one is not able to construct product terms as in the setting of a regression among observed variables. 

Despite that, the possibility to estimate latent interaction and quadratic terms is important. Indeed, for example, previous research (with observed variables) suggests that quadratic and interaction effects may "mask" or distort each other when predictors are correlated, which may lead to incorrect conclusions about the nature and direction of effects if not estimated simultaneously [@belzak_interaction_2019; @ganzach_misleading_1997]. Second, researchers in social and behavioral sciences should not have their theoretical models constrained by technical limitations—if theory suggests nonlinear effects exist, appropriate methods should be available to test these hypotheses rigorously [@oberauer_lewandowsky_2019]. Moreover, SEM accounts for random (classical) measurement error in the indicators of the variables entering the product by partitioning their variance into latent factors and residual error—provided the measurement model is correctly specified. This matters because observed product terms are typically less reliable than their components [@fisicaro_lautenschlager_1992; @bohrnstedt_marwell_1978]. Hence, estimating the interaction and quadratic terms at the latent level therefore yields predictors that, in principle, are corrected for attenuation from indicator error. Adding to that, Marsh et al. (2012) highlighted that a latent variable model contributes to higher statistical power, but this may not necessarily hold in general [@Fuller1987] and a more nuanced investigation is needed.

<!-- Add citation for the "minimizing bias in the estimates for the regression parameters in the structural model" ? -->

Hence, multiple frequentist-based methods have been proposed in recent years that reflect successive attempts to address specific limitations identified in previous methods [@kenny_judd_1984; @joreskog_yan_1996; @algina_moulder_2001; @klein_moosbrugger_2000; @klein_muthen_2007; @marsh_etall_2004; @bollen_1995; @wall_amemiya_gapi_2001; @wall_amemiya_2003; @wall_amemiya_2000; @mooijaart_bentler_2010; @mooijaart_satorra_2012; @boker_etall_2023]. However, these approaches differ substantially in their practical accessibility and in the assumptions required for their estimators to maintain desirable properties. For a brief theoretical overview of assumptions and expected performance, we refer the reader to @kelava_brandt_2022. Building on this, simulation studies [@marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @lonati_etall_2024] have provided empirical evaluations of these methods' performance, offering general guidelines and findings with respect to, for example, bias, type I error rate, power, and efficiency across the different approaches under multiple conditions. With a few notable exceptions, most of these approaches follow a joint ("system-wide") estimation method, meaning all parameters are jointly estimated. Indeed, that is the case for the more widely available^[In terms of software, XWITH command in Mplus and *nlsem*, *semTools*, *modsem* packages in R.] approaches: Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS), Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation (QML), and Product indicator (PI) approaches. 

In the PI approach, manifest products of linear indicators serve as indicators of a latent nonlinear factor—an interaction or a quadratic—that then enters the structural model [@kenny_judd_1984]. Early, constrained specifications identify this nonlinear measurement model by imposing algebraic relations that tie the PI measurement to the linear measurement model (e.g., equalities among loadings and moments derived under distributional assumptions); see @kelava_etall_2011 for a detailed overview. These constraints secured identification but restricted the model to assumptions that are often at violated with the nonnormality of indicator products. Subsequent work relaxed some of these restrictions, such as the Generalized Appended PI (GAPI) and the Unconstrained PI (UPI). Importantly, the UPI approach removed most constraints altogether, typically retaining only a minimal identifying restriction on the nonlinear factor mean [@kjell_etall_2024; @marsh_etall_2004; @kelava_etall_2011], and was later also further extended to structural models with both interaction and quadratic terms [@kelava_brandt_2009; @brandt_etall_2014]. Moreover, research has also explored optimal strategies for constructing product indicators and various centering approaches, including mean-centering, residual centering, and double mean centering [@marsh_etall_2004; @schoemann_jorgensen_2021; @kjell_etall_2024]. The distribution analytic approaches, LMS and QML, address the normality violations inherent in product indicator methods without creating measurement models for nonlinear terms [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_nonlinear_2014]. The LMS approach approximates non-normal distributions using mixtures of normal distributions, partitioning latent variables into subvectors for nonlinear and linear terms, then applying the EM algorithm to numerically integrate the weighted multivariate distributions [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_brandt_2022]. The QML approach offers a computationally efficient alternative in contrast to the LMS by replacing complex non-normal distributions with normal approximations that preserve the same mean and variance, creating normally distributed components that allow the use estimation by maximizing a quasi log-likelihood with minimal efficiency loss [@klein_muthen_2007]. 

@rosseel_etall_2025 recently proposed a novel approach for latent interaction and quadratic effects: the *local structural-after-measurement approach (LSAM)*^[This approach is closely connected to the more general two-stage method of moments (2SMM) [@wall_amemiya_2000; @wall_amemiya_2003]. As noted in @rosseel_etall_2025, and opposed to the 2SMM, the SAM does not require the structural part to be recursive, nor needs to distinguish in advance between endogenous and exogenous variables. Moreover, it is not needed to center the latent predictors involved in the nonlinear effects. Importantly, both do not require the latent predictors to follow a normal distribution.]. In fact, multiple SAM approaches were proposed in the literature for the estimation of nonlinear effects, such as interaction and product terms [@ng_chan_2020; @wall_amemiya_2003; @wall_amemiya_2000; @cox_kelcey_2021]. These methods follow similarly to the standard practice when all variables are observed, meaning quadratic and interaction terms are formed by multiplying the observed scores, but in this case factor scores are used. Importantly, factor scores retain measurement error, and their products are even less reliable than the main terms [@bohrnstedt_marwell_1978]. To address this, these SAM methods have been developed to explicitly accommodate two-way (and higher-order) interactions and power terms in the structural model while accounting for measurement error (see @rosseel_etall_2025 for a brief overview and limitations). In @rosseel_etall_2025, a small simulation study was conducted to evaluate the LSAM approach. The primary scope was limited, however, to examining the bias and variability of the point estimates involved in the interaction and quadratic terms under a limited set of conditions. Therefore, the aim of this paper is to further extend it by analyzing standard errors, coverage, type I error rate, and power.

A comprehensive evaluation of LSAM requires comparing its performance against the more established methods under multiple conditions that test the robustness of their underlying assumptions. Different approaches rely on distinct distributional assumptions when estimating interaction and quadratic terms, and the impact of violating these assumptions varies considerably across methods. As highlighted, previous simulation studies have demonstrated the negative impact that distributional misspecifications may have on LMS, QML, UPI, and other approaches [@marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @lonati_etall_2024]. Beyond distributional concerns, @rosseel_etall_2025 claimed that LMS, QML, and UPI also encounter "scalability" limitations. This entails that as the number of higher-order terms increases, their feasibility diminishes substantially. Specifically, the UPI becomes computationally impractical as more product indicators are needed, which inflates model matrices and creates convergence difficulties. Similarly, LMS requires numerical integration at each iteration, rapidly constraining feasibility to models containing relatively few latent variables. Although QML reduces computational demands compared to LMS, it should in principle be affected by scalability issues, though the extent remains unclear. These scalability concerns may partly explain why previous literature has largely focused on the elementary interaction model (EIM), with only a few studies examining complex models containing three or more interaction and product terms (e.g., Klein & Muthen, 2007; Brandt et al., 2014). In fact, little work has addressed the equations for models with multiple endogenous variables in LMS and QML, and implementing such models has required specific programming modifications [@kjell_etall_2024].

To investigate these concerns, we conduct two simulation studies comparing LSAM with LMS, UPI with double-mean centering, and QML. The first study examines performance across methods under varying distributional, reliability, and sample size conditions. The second study investigates scalability with the same varying conditions, but using a model that includes eight nonlinear terms to examine convergence rates and performance metrics to empirically assess whether scalability concerns are substantiated. For this second study we exclude LMS from the second study due to its known computational constraints with multiple nonlinear terms.

This paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we provide a brief overview of the methods under evaluation, including their distributional assumptions and implications for performance. We then present the simulation design, computational details, and performance measures for both studies. Following that, we report the results for each study separately before concluding with a general discussion that integrates our findings with previous simulation research.
